body_html:
An insurance estimate is the carrier's calculation of what covered damage should cost to repair, while the actual repair cost is what a contractor really charges to complete the work. The two often differ because of missed damage, outdated or average pricing, depreciation, code upgrades and hidden damage found during repairs. Policyholders can close the gap with supplements or appraisal.

Insurance estimate vs actual repair cost: the core difference

Your insurance estimate and your contractor's invoice are trying to describe the same repair, but they are built for different purposes. The carrier's estimate sets a claim value based on what the adjuster saw and documented, priced with estimating software. The actual repair cost reflects what it takes to finish the job on your specific property, at today's local prices, with whatever the crew finds once work begins.

When those two numbers do not match, you are the one left covering the difference unless you take action. Understanding why the gap exists is the first step toward getting it paid.

FactorInsurance estimateActual repair cost
Who prepares itCarrier adjuster or independent adjusterYour contractor
When it is madeUsually after one inspectionAs work is planned and completed
Pricing sourceEstimating software price listsReal supplier quotes and crew costs
Hidden damageNot included until foundIncluded once discovered
DepreciationDeducted from initial paymentNot part of the repair bill
Code upgradesMay be omittedRequired to pass inspection

How are insurance estimates created?

Most carrier estimates in Texas are written in Xactimate or Symbility. The adjuster inspects the property, takes photos and measurements, then builds a line-item estimate using the software's price list for your area.

  1. Inspection: the adjuster walks the property and notes visible damage.
  2. Measurements: roof squares, wall and floor areas and linear footage are recorded or pulled from aerial reports.
  3. Scope: each repair task is entered as a line item, such as tear-off, underlayment, shingles, drip edge and flashing.
  4. Pricing: the software applies regional unit prices for labor, materials and equipment.
  5. Adjustments: depreciation, deductible and any overhead and profit decisions are applied.
  6. Coverage review: items considered excluded or unrelated are removed.

The estimate is only as complete as the inspection behind it. If a damaged component is missed, it is not in the estimate and not in the payment.

Why is the insurance estimate lower than the repair cost?

A gap between the insurance estimate and the actual repair cost is common. These are the causes we see most often on Texas claims.

1. Missing scope

Items like starter course, ridge cap, drip edge, step flashing, pipe jacks, ventilation, gutter guards, interior paint on adjacent walls or detach-and-reset of fixtures are easy to leave off. Each small omission adds up. If you suspect the adjuster overlooked damage, read what to do if insurance missed roof damage.

2. Pricing that does not match the local market

Software prices are averages for a region and are updated periodically. After a major hailstorm, labor and material costs in Dallas, Fort Worth or Austin can climb faster than price lists reflect. Specialty materials, steep pitches and difficult access also drive real costs above standard line-item pricing. Learn more in how Xactimate pricing works in Texas.

3. Depreciation

Under a replacement cost policy, the first check is reduced by depreciation, which can make the payment look far lower than the repair cost. Much of that money may be recoverable after repairs. See recoverable depreciation explained.

4. Hidden damage

Rotted decking, wet insulation, damaged framing and water inside wall cavities often appear only after demolition starts. The original estimate cannot include what nobody could see.

5. Code requirements

Local building codes may require upgrades, such as specific underlayment, ventilation or drip edge, that were not on the original roof. Whether those costs are covered depends on your policy, often through ordinance or law coverage. Read ordinance and law coverage explained.

6. Repair vs replace decisions

An estimate may call for spot repairs where a contractor says full replacement is necessary because materials are discontinued, brittle or cannot be matched.

7. Overhead and profit

When a project needs a general contractor to coordinate multiple trades, overhead and profit is often a legitimate cost. Some estimates leave it out.

How to read your insurance estimate before comparing it to repair costs

Before you can compare an insurance estimate vs actual repair cost, you need to read the estimate correctly. Carrier estimates are long, but they follow a predictable structure.

  • Summary page: shows replacement cost value (RCV), depreciation, actual cash value (ACV), deductible and net payment.
  • Line items by area: each roof slope, elevation or room is listed with its own items.
  • Quantity column: squares, square feet, linear feet or each. Compare these with real measurements.
  • Unit price: the price per unit from the software's price list for your region and month.
  • Depreciation column: the age and percentage applied to each item, and whether it is recoverable.
  • Notes: adjuster comments explaining why something was included or excluded.

Read the notes carefully. Phrases like "repair only," "no damage observed" or "wear and tear" often explain the biggest differences between the insurance estimate and the actual repair cost. Those are exactly the points to address with photos and a contractor's written explanation.

Also check the price list date. If the estimate was written months ago and prices have since increased, ask the carrier to update pricing to the current month before you compare totals.

What does the actual repair cost include?

A contractor's price reflects everything needed to complete the job and pass inspection:

  • Labor, supervision and project management
  • Materials at current supplier pricing, including waste
  • Equipment rental, such as lifts, dumpsters and safety gear
  • Permits and inspections
  • Specialty subcontractors like electricians, HVAC techs and painters
  • Protection of landscaping, driveways and interiors
  • Cleanup and debris disposal
  • Code-required upgrades

Many of these appear in estimating software too, but they are frequently omitted, underquantified or priced differently. Our article on Xactimate vs contractor estimates compares the two approaches in depth.

An illustrative example of the gap

Consider a hypothetical hail claim on a 30-square asphalt roof. The carrier's estimate totals $16,500 replacement cost. Your contractor's bid is $21,000. Comparing them line by line reveals:

DifferenceWhy it matters
Waste factor lower than the roof's geometry requiresNot enough shingles priced for a cut-up hip roof
No step flashing or counter flashingFlashing generally must be replaced when the roof is replaced
Steep-pitch charges omittedRoofs above certain pitches require extra labor and safety equipment
Gutters and downspouts not includedVisible hail dents were not documented
No overhead and profitRoofing, gutter and painting trades need coordination

None of these numbers are data from a real claim; they illustrate how a few missing items can create a gap of several thousand dollars. Our roof square calculator helps you check squares, pitch and waste on your own roof.

How to close the gap between the estimate and the repair cost

  1. Get the full carrier estimate with line items, not just the summary page.
  2. Get a detailed contractor estimate that lists quantities and unit costs, ideally in the same format.
  3. Compare line by line. Mark missing items, different quantities and pricing differences.
  4. Document the difference with photos, measurements, code citations and supplier quotes.
  5. Submit a supplement in writing for missing or newly discovered items.
  6. Request re-inspection if the adjuster missed areas or the damage was hidden.
  7. Consider appraisal if the carrier agrees the loss is covered but will not agree on the amount.
Tip: Report hidden damage as soon as it is uncovered, and before it is repaired. Take photos while the wall or deck is still open so the adjuster can verify it.

Supplements are the normal way to add newly found damage. Our guide to supplemental insurance claims walks through the process.

Texas rules that matter when estimates fall short

Texas policyholders have some built-in protections. Under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542), insurers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days, accept or reject it within 15 business days of receiving requested information, and pay within 5 business days after accepting it. Chapter 541 prohibits unfair settlement practices, such as misrepresenting policy provisions.

Most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies also contain an appraisal clause for disputes over the amount of loss. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), appraisers decide the amount of loss and can assess damage, but not coverage questions. This is general information, not legal advice.

When does appraisal make sense?

Appraisal fits best when the carrier accepts that the loss is covered but the two sides disagree on how much it costs to repair. Typical examples include pricing disputes, quantity disputes, repair-versus-replace disagreements and missing scope.

It is less suited to pure coverage denials. Before you invoke, weigh the size of the gap against the cost. Our appraisal cost calculator compares likely costs with the amount in dispute.

Next steps for Texas property owners

A difference between the insurance estimate and the actual repair cost does not mean you must absorb it. Get the full estimate, compare it line by line with a detailed contractor bid, document what is missing and ask for a supplement. If the carrier still will not move on the amount, appraisal gives you a structured way to resolve the dispute without starting a lawsuit.

faqs.q: What happens if repairs cost more than the insurance estimate?
faqs.a: Tell your insurer before or as soon as the extra costs arise and submit a supplement with documentation, such as photos, invoices and an itemized contractor estimate. Carriers commonly revise estimates for newly discovered damage or missed items. If they will not agree on the amount, the appraisal clause in most Texas policies offers a way to resolve it.

faqs.q: Do I have to use the contractor my insurance company recommends?
faqs.a: Generally no. Most property policies let you choose your own qualified contractor. The carrier pays based on the covered amount of loss, not on which contractor you hire. Using your own contractor can help, because a detailed independent estimate gives you a basis to challenge a low carrier estimate.

faqs.q: Can I keep the difference if my repair costs less than the estimate?
faqs.a: Under a replacement cost policy, the insurer typically pays the lesser of the estimate or the amount actually spent once repairs are complete. If your repair costs less, the recoverable depreciation payment is usually reduced to match. The initial actual cash value payment is generally yours to keep, subject to any mortgage company requirements.

faqs.q: Why does my contractor's estimate not match the Xactimate estimate?
faqs.a: Contractors price jobs based on real supplier quotes, crew costs and site conditions, while Xactimate applies regional average unit prices to the items an adjuster documented. Differences in scope, quantities, waste, steep-pitch charges, code items and overhead and profit usually explain most of the gap between the two estimates.

faqs.q: Is a low insurance estimate a bad faith claim?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Estimates often differ in good faith because of missed items or pricing differences. Texas law prohibits certain unfair settlement practices, but whether conduct crosses that line depends on the facts. Start by documenting the gap and requesting a revision, and talk to a Texas attorney if you believe your rights were violated.
